title: Compacting responses: MISR
summary: The pattern generator makes the questions; now the chip must check the **answers**. Instead of storing millions of expected bits, BIST squeezes all responses into one short **signature** with an LFSR-like register — the **SISR** or **MISR**.
objectives: Explain why responses are compacted into a signature.
Compute a serial signature step by step and relate it to polynomial division.
Compute the next state of a MISR.
Explain aliasing and why unknown (X) values are dangerous.

blocks.md:
A logic BIST run applies thousands of patterns to circuits with thousands of outputs: **millions of response bits**. Storing all expected values on the chip would need a huge memory, and comparing them bit by bit a lot of logic.

The trick: feed all responses into a small register that mixes them into one short value — the **signature**. Only the final signature is compared with the expected **golden signature**, computed once by simulating the fault-free design.

blocks.alt: Responses go into a compactor that produces a signature compared with the golden one
blocks.caption: Response compaction

items.title: Simple idea 1: count the ones
items.md: Count how many 1s appear in the output stream. Cheap — but any error that turns one 0 into 1 **and** another 1 into 0 leaves the count unchanged and is missed.

items.title: Simple idea 2: count the transitions
items.md: Count how often the output changes 0→1 or 1→0. Also cheap, also blind to many error patterns.

items.title: The better idea: signature analysis
items.md: Feed the stream into an **LFSR** that keeps XOR-mixing it. Every bit influences the final state, and it is very unlikely that a wrong stream ends in the same state. This is what real BIST uses.

blocks.title: Compaction loses information
blocks.md: Millions of bits become a few dozen. So, in theory, a faulty circuit **could** produce the right signature. This is called **aliasing** — see 5.4. With a good register it is extremely unlikely.

Take the Galois LFSR of Topic 4 and add one XOR at its input: the data bit enters Q1 together with the feedback from Q4. This is a **serial-input signature register (SISR)**. It starts at 0000, then the circuit's output stream is clocked in, one bit per clock:

steps.title: Start: 0000
steps.md: The register is cleared before the test. The stream to compact is **11010011**.

steps.title: Bit 2 = 1 → 1100
steps.md: Q1 = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1; the old Q1 moves to Q2.

steps.title: Bit 5 = 0 → 1100
steps.md: Now Q4 = 1 is fed back: Q1 = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1; Q4 = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0.

steps.title: Bit 8 = 1 → signature 0100
steps.md: Q1 = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0; Q4 = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0. The final state **0100** is the signature of this stream.

tabs.label: Good stream
tabs.md: Stream **11010011** → signature **0100**. This is the golden signature.

tabs.label: One bit wrong
tabs.md: A defect flips the 5th bit: stream 1101**1**011. The register goes 1000, 1100, 0110, 1011, 0100, 0010, 1001, 0101 → signature **0101** ≠ 0100. **Fail** — the error is detected.

blocks.md: **Why it works — polynomial division.** Read the stream as a polynomial, first bit = highest power: 11010011 = x⁷ + x⁶ + x⁴ + x + 1. The SISR **divides** it by the register's polynomial p(x) = x⁴ + x³ + 1 and keeps the **remainder**. Qk holds the coefficient of xᵏ⁻¹, so Q1Q2Q3Q4 = 0100 means remainder = x.

blocks.caption: Division over GF(2): subtraction is XOR

blocks.title: A single wrong bit is always caught
blocks.md: One flipped bit adds xᵏ to the stream. Because p(x) ends with **+ 1**, it never divides xᵏ, so the remainder — the signature — always changes.

A real circuit has many outputs (or, in LBIST, many **scan chains**) producing bits in parallel. Putting an XOR in front of **every** stage lets one register take all of them in each clock: the **multiple-input signature register (MISR)**.

blocks.alt: 4-bit MISR with inputs D1 to D4
blocks.caption: A 4-bit MISR compacts 4 outputs at once
One wrong bit in clock 2 changes the final signature

blocks.title: In practice
blocks.md: MISRs are typically 16–64 bits wide. In LBIST, each scan chain feeds one MISR input (or a **space compactor** of XOR trees first reduces many chains to fewer inputs).

**Aliasing** happens when a faulty response still produces the golden signature. In terms of division: the **error pattern** (good stream ⊕ faulty stream) is a multiple of p(x), so it leaves the remainder unchanged.

tabs.label: An aliasing example
tabs.md: Error pattern 11001000 = x³ · p(x). Faulty stream: 11010011 ⊕ 11001000 = **00011011**. Its signature is also **0100** — three wrong bits, and the test still passes.

blocks.md: For long, random error streams the chance of aliasing in an n-bit register is about **2⁻ⁿ**:
That is why real MISRs are wide: with 32 bits, aliasing is practically impossible.

A much more practical danger is the **unknown value X**. Some flip-flops or outputs are not predictable in simulation: uninitialized memories or registers, buses with several drivers, analog blocks, signals crossing clock domains, slow (multicycle) paths at speed.

blocks.title: One X spoils the whole signature
blocks.md: An X entering the MISR is XOR-mixed into every later state. The final signature becomes unknown, so there is **no golden signature** to compare with. LBIST therefore needs **X-bounding** (fixing X sources in the design, e.g. initializing registers, blocking memory outputs) or **X-masking** (forcing known values in front of the MISR) — you will see both in the LBIST course.

questions.text: Why does BIST compact the responses into a signature instead of comparing every bit?
options: Storing millions of expected bits on the chip would need far too much memory and logic.
Signatures detect more faults than bit-by-bit comparison.
A MISR makes the circuit faster.
Responses cannot be compared bit by bit.

questions.text: The SISR of this topic (new Q1 = in ⊕ Q4, Q2 = Q1, Q3 = Q2, Q4 = Q3 ⊕ Q4) holds Q1Q2Q3Q4 = **0110**. The input bit is **1**. What is the next state?
A 4-bit MISR (Q1 = Q4 ⊕ D1, Q2 = Q1 ⊕ D2, Q3 = Q2 ⊕ D3, Q4 = Q3 ⊕ Q4 ⊕ D4) holds **1011**; the inputs are D1D2D3D4 = **0110**. Next state?
With a signature polynomial ending in + 1, a single wrong response bit always changes the signature.

options: A faulty circuit produces the same signature as the good one.
The golden signature is computed by simulation.
